bib.title: AI Agents: The Definitive Guide, Chapter 3. Advanced Planning, Reasoning, and Scalable Execution in Agents

question: How do RL (GRPO, GSPO, RULER, ART, rLLM) and test-time search (MCTS, AB-MCTS) let LLM agents improve from experience and spend compute adaptively?
hypothesis: Agent capability comes from learning dynamics and inference strategy, not model size.
contributions: Explains rewards, trajectories, rollouts, KL penalty, GRPO and GSPO with comparison tables
Walks through RULER + ART hybrid-reward training on Countdown with code
Explains MCTS and AB-MCTS (TreeQuest example) and rLLM workflow training

limits: Early Release: raw unedited text; full code is in the book's notebooks, not the chapter.
GRPO vs GSPO claims in Table 3-5 are asserted, sourced to Zheng et al. 2025, with no numbers.
Countdown run is a smoke test (64 scenarios, max 3 steps, 10 test items, no baseline, no seeds).
Table 3-5 says GRPO needs 'value-model surrogates' for MoE stability, though GRPO has no value model.
Section heading 'Why Absolute Scoring is Easier' contradicts its text, which argues relative comparison is easier.
Judge in AB-MCTS demo is the same model that writes the answer (gpt-4o).
practices: Compare several rollouts per task and use group-normalized rewards instead of absolute scores (GRPO/GSPO sections).
Add a KL penalty to keep the updated policy near the reference (Learning on a Leash).
Use RULER (LLM-as-judge ranking trajectories 0-1 on goal completion and efficiency) when rewards cannot be hand-coded.
For verifiable tasks use a deterministic reward; combine with RULER as a gated hybrid reward for reasoning quality (Example 3-11).
Keep ART training small while debugging (Example 3-12 comments).
Scale test-time compute with MCTS or AB-MCTS rather than model size (Test Time Compute section).
Use rLLM to train whole workflows (solver-judge, planner-executor) by subclassing Workflow, implementing run() and returning an Episode.
